Redside dace Clinostomus elongatus exhibits a maximum total length of 12 cm [Li = 12 cm] for adults, a size that is relatively modest among North American cyprinids and reflects its specialized headwater stream habitat. Field surveys have documented that females attain sexual maturation at a total length of 6 cm [Lp = 6 cm], at which point the wet weight at puberty is approximately 1.3 g [Wwp = approximately 1.3 g], reflecting the energetic investment required for gonadal development in this small-bodied minnow. The sustained thermal regime of 18 °C [T = 18 °C] in many of the cool, spring-fed tributaries of the Lake Erie basin appears to regulate key life history transitions. Under such conditions, the age at which free-swimming larvae emerge from the egg case is approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a duration that aligns closely with developmental rates observed in other Clinostomus species and reflects the moderate incubation temperatures characteristic of their native range at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C].

Quantification of reproductive output in Redside dace has been achieved through both field observations of gravid females and laboratory holding studies at a stable temperature of 18 °C. Females are capable of producing approximately 1526 eggs over the course of a single spawning season when maintained under these thermal conditions [Ri = approximately 1526 eggs over the course of a single spawning season when maintained under these thermal conditions], a fecundity that is distributed across multiple spawning events per year [F_R_i = multiple spawning events per year]. This high annual reproductive effort is typical of small-bodied cyprinids that experience significant juvenile mortality and must compensate through elevated fecundity. The maximum reproductive rate is sustained at the thermal optimum of 18 °C, where metabolic demands are balanced by adequate food availability in productive stream reaches. In cooler headwater sections, the spawning season may be truncated, reducing the total number of ova deposited per female compared to warmer downstream segments.

At the point of hatching, newly emerged prolarvae possess a minimal wet weight at birth of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], reflecting the small egg size typical of this species. The eggs themselves, based on measurements from the congener Clinostomus nasus which has a similar diameter of 1.5 mm, are transparent and adhesive, allowing them to attach to gravel substrates in fast-flowing riffles. Once the yolk sac is fully absorbed, the exotrophic larvae begin exogenous feeding on microcrustaceans and other zooplankton. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Redside dace, approximately 11.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 11.4 grams], represents a substantial increase from the larval stage and is achieved through a period of rapid somatic growth during the first year of life. This asymptotic body mass is consistent with the maximum recorded length of 12 cm [Li = 12 cm] and the species' allometric growth trajectory.

Longevity records from mark-recapture studies in Ohio and Pennsylvania indicate that the maximum lifespan for Clinostomus elongatus is approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] under natural stream conditions, with the oldest individuals typically found in stable groundwater-fed reaches where thermal variability is low and predation pressure from piscivorous fishes is minimal at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This lifespan, sustained at an average water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], is comparable to that of other small-bodied cyprinids in eastern North America and suggests a life history strategy that balances relatively late maturation with an extended reproductive window. Field data show that most mortality occurs during the first winter after hatching, after which annual survival rates increase substantially for sub-adult and adult individuals. The age at which females first spawn coincides with the attainment of 6 cm [Lp = 6 cm] total length, marking the transition to reproductive maturity.

Comparative analysis across the genus Clinostomus reveals that Redside dace occupies an intermediate position in terms of both maximum size and reproductive timing. While the closely related rosyside dace Clinostomus funduloides can reach slightly larger sizes, C. elongatus compensates with a higher relative fecundity when adjusted for body mass. The roughly ninefold increase in body mass between the 1.3 grams [Wwp = 1.3 grams] puberty threshold and the 11.4 grams [Wwi = 11.4 grams] adult maximum places C. elongatus at the higher end of the growth multiplier range for North American cyprinids, a pattern linked to its prolonged reproductive window and iteroparous spawning strategy. The consistent thermal regime of 18 °C across these life history benchmarks suggests that Redside dace is a stenothermic species whose phenology is tightly coupled to groundwater inputs. Conservation efforts should prioritize the protection of thermal refugia in headwater streams to maintain these critical physiological conditions.
